claims.claim: Elliot says one reason a world term goes unexplained is that the characters already know the concept even though it is foreign to the reader.
claims.source: Livia J. Elliot, 'The Puzzle Left Behind', Books Undone ep. 010 transcript, 2024
claims.quote: the characters may already know about those concepts

claims.claim: Elliot says a third reason a term goes unexplained is that the society has forgotten or misinterpreted its own history.
claims.source: Livia J. Elliot, 'The Puzzle Left Behind', Books Undone ep. 010 transcript, 2024
claims.quote: perhaps the society has forgotten or misinterpreted its own history

claims.claim: Elliot says the combination of the three kinds of omission is what adds realism to the world-building.
claims.source: Livia J. Elliot, 'The Puzzle Left Behind', Books Undone ep. 010 transcript, 2024
claims.quote: these three types of omission adds a level of realism

claims.claim: Elliot says the incomprehensible fragments of a world's history are what make its world-building stand out.
claims.source: Livia J. Elliot, 'The Puzzle Left Behind', Books Undone ep. 010 transcript, 2024
claims.quote: those bits of incomprehensible history are what makes the world-building pop

claims.claim: Elliot says Wolfe is an author who does not aid the reader by explaining concepts.
claims.source: Livia J. Elliot, 'The Puzzle Left Behind', Books Undone ep. 010 transcript, 2024
claims.quote: do not aid the reader by explaining concepts

claims.claim: Game designer Leo Hunt names the obscure and archaic language of The Book of the New Sun as a setting element he took into Vaults of Vaarn.
claims.quote: the obscure and archaic language that’s employed

claims.claim: Hunt names the melancholic weight of hundreds of extinguished civilisations on the present day as a Wolfe element carried into his game setting.
claims.quote: the melancholic weight of hundreds of extinguished civilisations

claims.claim: Novelist Daniel Polansky says the narrator's sins in Peace are hidden but identifiable by the scars they leave in his memory.
claims.quote: they can be identified by the scars they leave in his memory

claims.claim: Polansky says the narrative of Peace is riddled with ambiguities and contradictions and with holes the reader is encouraged to investigate.
claims.quote: riddled with ambiguities and contradictions, with holes we are encouraged to investigate

claims.claim: Polansky says a reader can miss the clues in Peace entirely and still be moved by the book.
claims.quote: possible to miss the subtle clues with which the book is filled

claims.claim: SF novelist Stephen Palmer says his favourite books are the ones where only a proportion of the meaning is on the surface, and names Wolfe as the model.
claims.quote: only a proportion of the meaning is on the surface

claims.claim: Palmer says his own Wolfe-influenced novel was written so that much of its meaning is concealed and must be teased out by the reader.
claims.quote: the meaning is concealed and has to be teased out by the reader

claims.claim: Critic Nick Gevers says every opening passage of The Book of the Long Sun stages a dialogue between a naive figure and one who holds privileged information.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 2000
claims.quote: a figure possessing privileged information, which he will only yield up

claims.claim: Gevers reads the opening passage of Nightside the Long Sun as a warning that interpreting the evidence given demands great care.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 2000
claims.quote: great care must be exercised in interpreting divine or authorial evidence

claims.claim: Gevers describes a formal conceit of The Book of the New Sun by which any fragment of the text contains the essence of the whole.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 2000
claims.quote: any fragment contains the essence of the whole

verdicts.trueWording: First, the characters may already know about those concepts
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the transcript; full sentence continues 'and, therefore, do not feel the need to explain them... even when they are foreign to the reader.' Both limbs (first of three reasons; foreign to the reader) supported. Page fetched raw with a browser UA, HTTP 200.

verdicts.trueWording: Or, third, perhaps the society has forgotten or misinterpreted its own history
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the page numbers it explicitly as the third of the tripartite answer ('Or, third,'). Raw page, HTTP 200.

verdicts.trueWording: The combination of these three types of omission adds a level of realism
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim as a contiguous substring; the page's full sentence ends '...to the world-building', supporting the claim's 'combination' and 'realism to the world-building' limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: those bits of incomprehensible history are what makes the world-building pop out of the page
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; 'pop out of the page' is the page's fuller phrasing of the claim's 'stand out'. Context is Elliot's own opinion about lost/incomprehensible history.

verdicts.trueWording: specific authors who, like Gene Wolfe, do not aid the reader by explaining concepts
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; Wolfe is named in the same clause as the exemplar. Claim's limbs fully supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Key setting elements like ... the obscure and archaic language that's employed
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe). It appears in the answer to the second interview question, which asks what each literary influence contributed to the world of Vaarn; Hunt lists it among 'Key setting elements' that are 'all these Vaarnish themes'. Byline/date confirmed: interview posted 27 August 2022, Bucolia.

verdicts.trueWording: the melancholic weight of hundreds of extinguished civilisations weighing upon the present day
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the page's continuation 'weighing upon the present day' supports the claim's 'on the present day', and the sentence's frame ('all these Vaarnish themes and more are found in Wolfe's magnum opus') supports 'carried into his game setting'.

verdicts.trueWording: His sins and shames are carefully hidden away ... but they can be identified by the scars they leave in his memory
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. 'Narrator' limb supported: the page describes Peace as 'the ramblings of one Alden Weer ... looking back on his life', and 'his memory' refers to Weer. Author bio on page confirms Polansky is a novelist ('author of four novels'). Reactormag fetched raw, HTTP 200.

verdicts.trueWording: The narrative of Weer's life is riddled with ambiguities and contradictions, with holes we are encouraged to investigate
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. The page's subject is 'the narrative of Weer's life' rather than the literal words 'the narrative of Peace', but Peace is Weer's retrospective account of that life, so the claim's subject is the same thing; 'we are encouraged' supports 'the reader is encouraged'.

verdicts.trueWording: altogether possible to miss the subtle clues with which the book is filled ... and to still walk away touched by the book
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Both limbs supported: 'to miss them altogether' (miss entirely) and 'still walk away touched by the book' (still be moved). The page frames this as conditional on being ignorant of Wolfe's reputation, which does not contradict the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: My favourite books are usually the ones where only a proportion of the meaning is on the surface
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim on the page and the first limb holds (though the page says 'usually'). The second limb fails: in the same paragraph Palmer expressly disclaims Wolfe as a model - 'I didn't copy his style ... nor did I copy his techniques' and 'I wanted my novels to have many hidden depths, not in imitation of Gene Wolfe but because that was what interested, indeed, compelled me.' He calls Wolfe an influence and BotNS 'like manna to me', but never the model. Page confirms 'SF writer Stephen Palmer', 'author of nine science fiction novels', 4 August 2015.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: names Wolfe as the model - the page has Palmer explicitly denying imitation of Wolfe's style or techniques, and saying his taste for hidden depths was 'not in imitation of Gene Wolfe'

verdicts.trueWording: a great proportion of the meaning is concealed and has to be teased out by the reader
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. 'His own Wolfe-influenced novel' supported: 'The other one of my novels that is much influenced by Gene Wolfe is Urbis Morpheos'; 'much of its meaning' = 'a great proportion of the meaning'.

verdicts.trueWording: each opening passage features a dialogue between a more-or-less naive individual and a figure possessing privileged information
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (page uses 'naive' with diaeresis). 'Every opening passage' supported by 'each opening passage', in a paragraph explicitly about 'the beginnings and endings of the four volumes' of Long Sun. Byline confirmed on page: 'By Nick Gevers', 5 September 2000, Ultan's Library.

verdicts.trueWording: The opening passage of Nightside has been a warning - from God or Wolfe - that great care must be exercised in interpreting divine or authorial evidence
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the 'warning' and 'opening passage of Nightside' limbs are the page's own words.

verdicts.trueWording: the conceit that its text is like a hologram: any fragment contains the essence of the whole
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the page's frame 'One of the numerous formal devices of The Book of the New Sun is the conceit...' supports 'formal conceit of The Book of the New Sun'.
